title: Preeclampsia: Blood Pressure Plus Organ Danger
bottomLine: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy/postpartum hypertensive disorder with maternal organ and placental risk; proteinuria is not required when other severe features are present. Severe persistent hypertension, severe headache, visual symptoms, RUQ/epigastric pain, pulmonary edema, neurologic change or worsening labs require urgent obstetric escalation.
recognize: New hypertension after 20 weeks or postpartum
Severe headache, vision change, RUQ/epigastric pain, dyspnea, hyperreflexia/clonus
Thrombocytopenia, liver injury, kidney dysfunction or pulmonary edema can indicate severe disease
Preeclampsia can first appear postpartum
assess: Repeat BP using correct cuff/position and follow severe-BP confirmation protocol
Neuro symptoms/reflexes, lung sounds, edema and urine output
Fetal assessment and CBC, creatinine, liver tests, urine protein as ordered
actions: Escalate severe BP or severe features promptly
Administer ordered rapid antihypertensive therapy for acute severe hypertension
Use seizure precautions and magnesium sulfate when ordered for seizure prophylaxis/treatment
Prepare for delivery decisions made by the obstetric team when maternal/fetal status requires
diagnostics: Proteinuria supports diagnosis but absence does not exclude preeclampsia with other qualifying organ findings
Trend platelets, renal/liver markers and fetal status
medicationSafety: Magnesium sulfate prevents/treats eclamptic seizures; it is not primarily an antihypertensive
Antihypertensive selection is pregnancy-specific
NSAID use postpartum may require individualized review in selected hypertension/kidney contexts
teaching: Teach postpartum warning signs and that preeclampsia can develop after discharge
Home BP monitoring and follow-up should follow the obstetric plan
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN maternity practice varies by state/facility. The practical nurse can recognize severe features, obtain accurate BP/focused data, administer ordered medication within scope, institute seizure safety and escalate immediately.
examTrap: Ruling out preeclampsia because urine protein is negative despite severe hypertension and neurologic symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Preeclampsia is pressure plus organ/placental risk—not a protein-only disease.
sourceBasis: ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia

title: Magnesium Sulfate: Seizure Prevention With Respiratory and Reflex Monitoring
bottomLine: Magnesium sulfate is used for eclampsia seizure prevention/treatment and selected fetal neuroprotection protocols. Monitor respiratory rate, level of consciousness, reflexes, urine output and ordered magnesium level; reduced renal clearance increases toxicity risk. Respiratory depression, marked loss of reflexes or severe somnolence requires stopping/holding per protocol and urgent escalation, with calcium gluconate available as the antidote.
recognize: Expected effects can include warmth, flushing and nausea
Toxicity can progress from depressed reflexes to respiratory depression and cardiac effects
Oliguria raises toxicity risk because magnesium is renally cleared
assess: Respiratory rate/effort, SpO2, mental status, deep tendon reflexes and urine output
Verify infusion rate/concentration using high-alert medication checks
Trend serum magnesium when ordered or clinical toxicity is suspected
actions: Maintain seizure precautions and infusion monitoring
Stop/hold according to emergency protocol for toxicity and notify obstetric team
Prepare/administer IV calcium gluconate when ordered for significant toxicity
Support airway/ventilation if respiratory depression occurs
diagnostics: Clinical monitoring is central; serum level interpretation must be tied to symptoms and renal function
medicationSafety: Magnesium and other CNS/neuromuscular depressants can compound respiratory weakness
Calcium gluconate is the standard reversal agent for serious magnesium toxicity
teaching: Explain expected warmth/flushing and instruct the patient to report difficulty breathing, chest symptoms or profound weakness
scopeAndDelegation: Magnesium infusion initiation/titration authority varies by setting. PN/LVN must follow high-alert medication and maternity policy and immediately report toxicity signs.
examTrap: Continuing magnesium despite new respiratory depression because the serum level has not returned yet.
sourceBasis: ACOG Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia Guidance

title: Postpartum Hemorrhage: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin
bottomLine: Postpartum hemorrhage is a resuscitation emergency. Quantify blood loss, assess uterine tone and source, call for help early, provide uterine massage for atony, empty the bladder, administer oxytocin/other uterotonics and tranexamic acid as ordered, obtain large-bore access/blood products, and reassess perfusion continuously.
recognize: Atony: boggy enlarged uterus with heavy bleeding
Trauma: persistent bleeding despite firm uterus
Retained tissue can prevent contraction
Coagulopathy can cause diffuse oozing
Tachycardia, pallor, dizziness and hypotension indicate significant loss
assess: Fundal tone/position, lochia and quantitative blood loss
BP/HR/perfusion, mental status, urine output
Inspect for laceration/hematoma signs and retained tissue risk
Trend CBC/coagulation/fibrinogen and crossmatch as ordered
actions: Activate obstetric hemorrhage protocol
Massage a boggy uterus and address bladder distention
Give oxytocin first-line and additional uterotonics based on contraindications/order
Administer tranexamic acid when ordered and clinically indicated
Prepare for transfusion and procedural/surgical hemorrhage control
diagnostics: Clinical bleeding and hemodynamics drive response; do not wait for hemoglobin to fall
Bedside ultrasound and labs may help identify retained tissue or coagulopathy
medicationSafety: Methylergonovine is generally avoided with hypertension/preeclampsia
Carboprost is generally avoided in asthma
Misoprostol effects include fever/shivering
Tranexamic acid has timing and thrombotic considerations
redFlags: Firm uterus with continued brisk bleeding
teaching: After discharge, seek urgent care for soaking pads rapidly, large clots with weakness, syncope, dyspnea, chest pain or worsening bleeding
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN role depends on maternity setting; immediate recognition, uterine/perfusion assessment, protocol activation and ordered uterotonic/resuscitation support are essential. Surgical/device escalation is team directed.
examTrap: Repeatedly massaging a firm uterus while ignoring a laceration or expanding hematoma.
oneLinePearl: PPH: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin—resuscitate while finding the source.

title: Placenta Previa vs Abruption: Bleeding Patterns Change the Exam
bottomLine: Third-trimester bleeding requires rapid maternal/fetal assessment. Placenta previa classically causes painless bleeding and requires placental location before digital cervical examination; abruption more often causes painful bleeding, uterine tenderness/rigidity and fetal compromise, and bleeding can be concealed.
recognize: Previa: painless bright bleeding may occur
Abruption: abdominal/back pain, uterine tenderness or hypertonicity, contractions and fetal distress
Visible blood loss can underestimate abruption severity
assess: Maternal BP/HR/perfusion, bleeding amount, pain and uterine tone
Fetal heart rate and gestational status
Review previa/cesarean history, trauma, hypertension and substance risks
actions: Stabilize maternal circulation and activate obstetric response
Avoid digital vaginal examination until placenta previa is excluded
Obtain ordered IV access/labs/blood and prepare for delivery if maternal or fetal instability requires
diagnostics: Abruption can be a clinical diagnosis even with nondiagnostic ultrasound
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant status affects hemorrhage management
Rh-negative pregnant patients may require Rh immune globulin depending on the clinical situation
redFlags: Severe pain with little visible blood
teaching: Any significant pregnancy bleeding, severe abdominal pain or decreased fetal movement needs prompt obstetric evaluation
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN obtains focused maternal/fetal data and supports emergency care. Digital cervical examinations and delivery decisions follow obstetric policy and clinician authorization.
examTrap: Performing a digital vaginal examination on a patient with painless third-trimester bleeding before placental location is known.
oneLinePearl: Previa: painless and no digital exam until located; abruption: pain/tenderness and concealed loss can be severe.

title: PROM and PPROM: Ruptured Membranes Mean Infection and Cord Risk
bottomLine: When membranes rupture before labor, determine gestational age, fetal status, infection signs, labor and cord risk. Limit unnecessary digital vaginal examinations because they increase infection risk, and promptly escalate fever, uterine tenderness, foul fluid, fetal tachycardia, cord prolapse or nonreassuring fetal status.
recognize: Gush or persistent leaking fluid
PPROM occurs before 37 weeks
Complications include infection, cord accident, placental abruption and preterm birth
assess: Maternal temperature/vitals and uterine tenderness
Fluid characteristics and fetal heart rate/movement
Contractions, gestational age and cord-prolapse risk
actions: Confirm rupture using approved sterile/speculum-based methods
Avoid repeated digital examinations unless clinically necessary for delivery management
Administer latency antibiotics, corticosteroids, magnesium or GBS prophylaxis as ordered according to gestational age
Escalate infection or fetal compromise
diagnostics: Pooling/ferning/pH or validated biochemical tests may confirm rupture
Ultrasound fluid volume supports but does not alone prove membrane rupture
medicationSafety: Antibiotic and antenatal corticosteroid regimens are gestational-age and circumstance specific
Tocolysis is selective and not appropriate with infection or certain contraindications
teaching: Report leaking fluid, fever, foul odor, bleeding, contractions or decreased fetal movement immediately
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN maternity responsibilities depend on setting; avoid restricted cervical exams and escalate suspected rupture/complications promptly.
examTrap: Performing frequent digital cervical examinations after PPROM to see whether labor is progressing.
oneLinePearl: Ruptured membranes: gestation, fetus, infection, cord—and minimize digital exams.
sourceBasis: ACOG Practice Bulletin 217 Prelabor Rupture of Membranes and Updates

title: Preterm Labor: Contractions Plus Cervical Change Before Term
bottomLine: Preterm labor is regular uterine activity with cervical change before 37 weeks. The goal is not to stop every contraction indefinitely; identify true labor and complications, give antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium for fetal neuroprotection and short-term tocolysis when indicated, and transfer to appropriate neonatal/obstetric care when needed.
recognize: Regular tightening, pelvic pressure, low backache, cramping or change in discharge
Cervical change distinguishes true labor from many false-labor presentations
PPROM, bleeding, infection or fetal compromise changes management
assess: Contraction pattern, gestational age, cervical evaluation by authorized clinician
Membrane status, bleeding, infection signs
Fetal heart rate and movement
actions: Notify obstetric team and follow preterm-labor pathway
Administer antenatal corticosteroids and other gestational-age-specific therapy as ordered
Tocolysis may be used briefly in selected cases to allow steroids/transfer
Prepare for delivery if contraindications to delaying birth are present
diagnostics: Cervical length/fetal fibronectin can help risk stratification in selected patients but do not replace clinical assessment
medicationSafety: Tocolytics have agent-specific maternal/fetal contraindications
Magnesium for neuroprotection is not a routine long-term tocolytic
Corticosteroids can transiently raise glucose
teaching: Report contractions, leaking fluid, bleeding, pelvic pressure and decreased fetal movement promptly
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN supports monitoring and ordered medication within maternity policy. Cervical diagnosis and tocolysis/delivery decisions are obstetric-team directed.
examTrap: Assuming bedrest is a universal evidence-based treatment for preventing preterm birth.
oneLinePearl: Preterm labor care buys useful time only when delaying birth is safe.
sourceBasis: ACOG Management and Prevention of Preterm Birth Guidance

title: Fetal Heart Rate: Baseline, Variability, Decelerations, Context
bottomLine: Interpret fetal heart rate as a pattern, not one isolated deceleration: baseline, variability, accelerations/decelerations, contraction pattern and clinical context all matter. A clearly abnormal or worsening pattern requires intrauterine resuscitative measures and prompt obstetric escalation rather than repeatedly charting the strip without action.
recognize: Moderate variability is generally reassuring of intact fetal neurologic/oxygenation status at that moment
Early decelerations commonly track head compression
Variable decelerations suggest cord compression
Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency when recurrent
Prolonged bradycardia demands immediate evaluation
assess: Maternal BP/pulse, position, uterine activity, oxytocin rate, recent medications, bleeding and membrane status
FHR baseline/variability/deceleration type/frequency and recovery
Check for cord prolapse after sudden bradycardia following membrane rupture when appropriate
actions: Reposition the patient and correct maternal hypotension/hypoxemia when present
Reduce/stop oxytocin for tachysystole or concerning pattern according to protocol
Give IV fluid bolus and other intrauterine resuscitation as ordered
Escalate persistent severe abnormality for operative delivery evaluation
diagnostics: Electronic fetal monitoring is interpreted using the current ACOG framework; one pattern must be read in clinical context
medicationSafety: Oxytocin can cause uterine tachysystole and fetal compromise
Supplemental oxygen is not a universal treatment for fetal decelerations in a normally oxygenated mother
redFlags: Absent variability with recurrent late/variable decelerations
teaching: Explain position changes and monitoring without implying every deceleration means fetal injury
scopeAndDelegation: FHR interpretation and oxytocin management may require RN-level obstetric competency depending on state/facility. PN/LVN must recognize obvious deterioration, obtain help and perform authorized supportive actions rather than independently managing a high-risk tracing outside scope.
examTrap: Giving oxygen automatically for every deceleration to a mother with normal oxygen saturation instead of correcting the actual cause.
oneLinePearl: FHR is pattern + contractions + mother + context.
sourceBasis: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline 10 Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring: Interpretation and Management

title: Umbilical Cord Prolapse: Lift the Presenting Part and Move to Delivery
bottomLine: Sudden profound fetal bradycardia or recurrent severe variable decelerations after membrane rupture can signal cord prolapse. Call for emergency help, manually elevate the presenting part off the cord when trained/authorized, position to reduce compression, stop oxytocin, avoid unnecessary cord handling and prepare for immediate delivery.
recognize: Visible/palpable cord after membrane rupture
Abrupt fetal bradycardia or severe variables
Risk increases when the presenting part is high or malpresentation/polyhydramnios is present
assess: Fetal heart rate and membrane-rupture timing
Presenting part/cord assessment by authorized clinician
Maternal position and contraction/oxytocin status
actions: Activate obstetric emergency and stay with patient
Relieve cord compression manually and/or with positioning according to protocol
Stop oxytocin and support maternal hemodynamics
Prepare for emergent cesarean or rapid vaginal birth if imminent and appropriate
diagnostics: This is a clinical emergency; do not delay delivery for imaging
medicationSafety: Tocolytic may be used selectively if delivery is delayed under obstetric direction
Do not administer routine medications that postpone emergency delivery
teaching: During the emergency, use concise reassurance and explain that rapid positioning and delivery are needed to protect fetal oxygenation
scopeAndDelegation: Cord-prolapse management is an obstetric emergency. PN/LVN actions are defined by unit policy and competency; immediate activation of qualified obstetric staff is mandatory.
examTrap: Trying to push the prolapsed cord back into the uterus.
oneLinePearl: Cord prolapse: relieve compression and deliver fast.

title: Shoulder Dystocia: Call, Maneuvers, No Fundal Pressure
bottomLine: Shoulder dystocia is an unpredictable birth emergency after the fetal head delivers and shoulders do not. Call for help immediately, note the time, assist with the ordered sequence of maneuvers such as McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, and never apply fundal pressure because it can worsen impaction.
recognize: Difficulty delivering shoulders after head, retraction/turtle sign may occur
Risk factors have poor predictive value, so preparedness matters
Maternal hemorrhage/laceration and neonatal brachial plexus or hypoxic injury can follow
assess: Time from head delivery and maternal/fetal status
Post-delivery maternal bleeding/trauma
Newborn movement, breathing and injury assessment
actions: Call obstetric, neonatal and anesthesia help
McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure as directed
Assist with additional maneuvers and prepare for neonatal resuscitation/PPH management
Document maneuvers and timing objectively
diagnostics: Diagnosis is clinical during delivery; post-birth evaluation assesses maternal and neonatal injury
medicationSafety: Do not use oxytocin or fundal pressure as a solution to an impacted shoulder
teaching: After stabilization, explain what occurred and the need for maternal/newborn follow-up without assigning blame
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN assists the obstetric emergency team according to unit competency. Internal maneuvers are performed by authorized obstetric clinicians.
examTrap: Applying fundal pressure to force the shoulder under the pubic bone.
oneLinePearl: Shoulder dystocia: help, McRoberts/suprapubic, never fundal pressure.

title: Gestational Diabetes: Glucose Control Protects Parent and Baby
bottomLine: Gestational diabetes increases risk of hypertensive disease, fetal overgrowth, birth complications and neonatal hypoglycemia. Management starts with nutrition/activity and glucose monitoring; medication is added when targets are not met. After delivery, insulin resistance falls rapidly and postpartum diabetes screening/future risk counseling matter.
recognize: Often asymptomatic and diagnosed by screening
Poor control increases fetal growth and neonatal metabolic risk
GDM increases future type 2 diabetes risk
assess: Fasting/postprandial glucose according to the obstetric plan
Nutrition/activity, medication adherence and hypoglycemia
Fetal growth/antenatal surveillance as ordered
actions: Reinforce individualized nutrition and activity plan
Administer insulin or other approved therapy as ordered
Coordinate intrapartum glucose plan and neonatal glucose surveillance
Ensure postpartum diabetes testing is arranged
diagnostics: Screening/diagnostic strategies are protocol-specific; postpartum testing evaluates persistent dysglycemia
medicationSafety: Insulin needs can change rapidly during pregnancy and drop after delivery
Oral-agent use is individualized; do not assume every noninsulin diabetes drug is pregnancy appropriate
teaching: Glucose technique, hypoglycemia treatment, meal plan, postpartum testing and long-term diabetes prevention
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN reinforces the plan and administers ordered therapy; dose changes and obstetric surveillance decisions are clinician-directed.
examTrap: Assuming gestational diabetes disappears permanently after birth and no postpartum screening is needed.
oneLinePearl: GDM ends the pregnancy risk, not the future diabetes risk.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Postpartum Endometritis: Fever, Uterine Tenderness, Foul Lochia
bottomLine: Postpartum uterine infection commonly presents with fever, uterine/fundal tenderness, malaise and sometimes foul-smelling lochia. Assess for sepsis and alternative sources, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics as ordered, maintain hydration/pain control and evaluate retained tissue or abscess when the patient fails to improve.
recognize: Postpartum fever with uterine tenderness
Foul lochia may occur but is not required
Cesarean birth, prolonged rupture/labor and intraamniotic infection increase risk
assess: Vitals/perfusion, uterine tenderness/involution, lochia, incision, urine and breast symptoms
Sepsis signs and hydration
CBC/cultures/imaging as ordered if severe or not improving
actions: Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly
Support fluids, analgesia and mobility
Escalate sepsis, persistent fever, abscess or retained-product concern
diagnostics: Diagnosis is often clinical; cultures/imaging are reserved for selected severe or refractory cases
medicationSafety: Antibiotic regimen must cover polymicrobial postpartum infection and account for allergies/renal function
teaching: Report fever, worsening uterine/pelvic pain, foul discharge, wound changes or feeling systemically ill after discharge
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs postpartum assessment, gives ordered antibiotics and reports sepsis or failure to improve. Source-control decisions are obstetric-team directed.
examTrap: Assuming postpartum fever is normal milk 'coming in' without assessing uterine, wound, urine, breast and systemic infection signs.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum fever plus uterine tenderness means endometritis until evaluated.

title: Newborn First Hours: Warmth, Breathing, Glucose, Feeding, Jaundice
bottomLine: Newborn transition requires attention to temperature, respiratory effort/color, glucose risk, feeding, infection and bilirubin trajectory. Jaundice in the first 24 hours or bilirubin near treatment thresholds requires prompt evaluation; visual estimation alone is not adequate for high-risk decisions.
recognize: Respiratory distress: grunting, flaring, retractions, central cyanosis or apnea
Hypoglycemia risk includes infants of diabetic parents, growth restriction, large size, prematurity and symptoms
Jaundice progresses cephalocaudally but skin appearance cannot quantify bilirubin reliably
assess: Temperature, respiratory effort, color, feeding, urine/stool and weight
Glucose screening according to newborn risk protocol
Transcutaneous/serum bilirubin and age in hours with gestational/risk factors
actions: Maintain warmth and skin-to-skin when stable
Support early feeding and glucose treatment per protocol
Escalate respiratory distress or symptomatic hypoglycemia
Use age-specific bilirubin follow-up/phototherapy thresholds
diagnostics: Bilirubin treatment decisions use measured level, age in hours, gestation and neurotoxicity risk factors
Direct antiglobulin/blood type and hemolysis tests are selected when indicated
medicationSafety: Glucose gel is protocol-driven for selected asymptomatic low glucose
Phototherapy needs eye/temperature/hydration/feeding monitoring according to protocol
teaching: Feeding cues/frequency, jaundice and dehydration warning signs, safe sleep on the back on a firm flat surface without soft bedding, and prompt newborn follow-up
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN newborn care depends on setting. Accurate transition assessment and escalation of respiratory, glucose or jaundice abnormalities are essential.
examTrap: Estimating severe jaundice only by skin color and delaying a bilirubin measurement.
oneLinePearl: Newborn: breathe, warm, feed, glucose when at risk, measure bilirubin when it matters.
